lessons.title: Monro–Kellie & ICP

levels.kid:
Your brain lives inside your skull, and the skull is like a hard box that cannot stretch.

Inside the box are three things:
- the brain itself
- blood
- a clear, watery fluid that cushions the brain

The box is always full. So if one thing gets bigger, like a bump of blood or a swollen brain, something else has to squeeze out to make room. At first, some fluid and blood can slip out, and everything is okay.

But if the bump keeps growing, there is no more room. The pressure inside the box goes up. That pressure can squash the brain, so doctors watch it very carefully.
levels.hs:
The **Monro–Kellie doctrine** says the skull is a rigid box with a fixed volume. Inside are three things: **brain tissue (about 80%)**, **blood (about 10%)** and **cerebrospinal fluid, CSF (about 10%)**. Their total volume stays constant.

When something new takes up space (a blood clot, a tumor, brain swelling), the body first **compensates**: CSF is pushed down into the spinal canal and venous blood is squeezed out of the head. While this reserve lasts, the pressure barely rises.

Once the reserve is used up, even a tiny extra volume makes **intracranial pressure (ICP)** shoot up. Normal ICP in a resting adult is about **5-15 mmHg**; guidelines for severe head injury treat sustained values above about **22 mmHg**.

Pressure matters because blood has to be pushed into the brain against it. **Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) = mean arterial pressure (MAP) - ICP.** If ICP rises or blood pressure falls, CPP drops and the brain becomes starved of oxygen.

Signs of raised ICP:
- headache, often worse lying down or in the morning
- vomiting
- blurred vision and swollen optic discs (**papilledema**)
- drowsiness
- late: **Cushing's triad** (high blood pressure, slow heart rate, irregular breathing)
levels.college:
**Pressure-volume relationship.** Adding volume to the cranial vault produces an exponential pressure curve. On the flat part, compliance (change in volume divided by change in pressure) is high: CSF displacement into the spinal subarachnoid space and compression of the venous sinuses buffer the new volume. At the 'knee' of the curve compliance is exhausted, and small additions (a cough, a rise in CO2, a few millilitres of clot) cause large ICP spikes. Elastance is the inverse of compliance.

**ICP waveform.** A normal pulse waveform has three peaks: **P1** (percussion wave, arterial pulsation), **P2** (tidal wave, reflecting brain compliance) and **P3** (dicrotic wave, aortic valve closure). Normally P1 > P2 > P3. When **P2 rises above P1**, compliance is poor, even if the mean ICP still looks acceptable. **Lundberg A (plateau) waves** are sustained rises to very high pressures lasting minutes and signal exhausted compensation; B waves are shorter rhythmic oscillations.

**Cerebral blood flow (CBF) control.** Autoregulation keeps CBF roughly constant over a range of MAP (classically about 50-150 mmHg, but individually variable and often impaired after injury). CO2 is a powerful vasodilator: hypercapnia raises cerebral blood volume and ICP; hypocapnia does the opposite, which is why brief hyperventilation lowers ICP.

**Brain edema types:**
- **Vasogenic**: blood-brain barrier breakdown, fluid in white matter around tumors and abscesses; responds to corticosteroids.
- **Cytotoxic**: cells swell from failed ion pumps in ischemia or trauma; does not respond to steroids.
- **Interstitial**: CSF forced across the ventricular lining in obstructive hydrocephalus.

**Hydrocephalus** adds CSF volume and is a reversible cause of raised ICP if drained.
levels.phd:
Alexander Monro (1783) and George Kellie (1824) argued that the intact skull contains an incompressible, constant volume; George Burrows later added CSF as the third, exchangeable component. The doctrine is a useful first approximation with known limits: infants with open sutures and fontanelles can expand the vault, the spinal dural sac is distensible, and venous blood volume is highly dynamic.

**Quantifying compliance.** Marmarou's **pressure-volume index (PVI)** is the volume that raises ICP tenfold, derived from bolus injection or withdrawal; normal adults sit around 25 mL. Because bolus testing carries infection risk, continuous indices are preferred. The **RAP index** (correlation between pulse amplitude and mean ICP) approaches +1 on the steep part of the curve and falls toward zero or negative near terminal vasoplegia, when the vascular bed can no longer transmit pulsations.

**Autoregulation as a continuous signal.** The **pressure reactivity index (PRx)** is a moving correlation coefficient between slow waves of MAP and ICP. With intact reactivity, a rise in MAP triggers vasoconstriction and blood volume falls, so the correlation is negative or near zero; passive, non-reactive vessels give positive PRx, which is associated with mortality. Plotting PRx against CPP often reveals a U-shaped curve whose minimum defines an individual **optimal CPP (CPPopt)**. Trials such as COGiTATE have tested whether targeting CPPopt is feasible and safe, but outcome benefit is not yet established.

**Pressure is not uniform.** Transtentorial and interhemispheric gradients exist, especially with focal masses, so a parenchymal probe on one side may under-read pressure near a lesion on the other. Compartment-level thinking explains why temporal and posterior fossa lesions can cause herniation at 'normal' global ICP.

**Idiopathic intracranial hypertension** shows that venous outflow matters: transverse sinus stenosis can act as a feedback loop, and venous sinus stenting is an emerging treatment in selected patients.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, the ICP number is one input, never the whole story. An attending integrates the trend, the waveform, the CT and, above all, the clinical examination. A patient with a large temporal contusion can herniate with an ICP in the high teens because the mass sits right next to the uncus and brainstem; conversely, a short spike during suctioning means little if it settles quickly.

**First, fix the simple things that raise ICP:**
- head of bed elevated to about 30 degrees, head midline
- loosen a tight cervical collar or tube ties that block jugular venous outflow
- treat fever, pain, agitation and ventilator dyssynchrony
- keep oxygenation normal and CO2 in the normal range
- avoid hypotension and hyponatremia (low sodium shifts water into the brain)
- look for and treat seizures, including non-convulsive ones on EEG

**Then ask whether there is a surgical answer.** Is there a clot to evacuate? Is there hydrocephalus that an external ventricular drain would relieve? Hydrocephalus is one of the most reversible causes of a rising ICP, and the drain both measures and treats.

**Pitfalls:**
- Lumbar puncture in a patient with a mass lesion or obstructive hydrocephalus can create a downward pressure gradient and cause herniation. Image first when there are focal signs, papilledema or reduced consciousness.
- Opening pressure on LP is only valid lying on the side with legs relaxed.
- In idiopathic intracranial hypertension the danger is permanent vision loss, not herniation, so serial visual fields and fundus examination drive decisions.
- In infants, a tense bulging fontanelle and rapidly increasing head circumference are the clues.

Think of ICP as a symptom. The job is to find out why it is high.

keyPoints: Skull volume is fixed: brain about 80%, blood about 10%, CSF about 10% (Monro–Kellie).
Compensation (CSF and venous blood displacement) runs out at the knee of an exponential pressure-volume curve.
Normal adult ICP is about 5-15 mmHg; severe TBI guidelines treat sustained ICP above about 22 mmHg.
CPP = MAP - ICP.
P2 above P1 on the ICP waveform signals poor compliance.
Vasogenic edema responds to steroids; cytotoxic edema does not.

test.q: The Monro–Kellie doctrine states that:
choices: Brain, blood and CSF share a fixed total intracranial volume
CSF volume stays constant whatever the brain or blood volume
ICP is independent of how much blood is inside the skull
The adult skull expands slightly to fit brain swelling
test.explain: In the rigid adult skull the three components have a fixed sum, so an increase in one must be offset by a decrease in another.

test.q: Which component makes up most of the intracranial volume?
test.explain: Brain parenchyma is roughly 80% of the volume; blood and CSF are about 10% each.

test.q: Normal ICP in a resting adult is about:
test.explain: About 5-15 mmHg is normal; sustained values above about 22 mmHg are treated in severe TBI.

test.q: Cerebral perfusion pressure = mean arterial pressure minus ___.
test.explain: CPP = MAP - ICP, so a rising ICP or falling blood pressure both reduce brain perfusion.

test.q: What happens first when a small mass starts to grow inside the skull?
choices: ICP rises immediately and steeply with each added mL
The brain shrinks permanently to make room for it
Arterial blood flow stops to make space for it
CSF and venous blood are displaced out of the head
test.explain: Early on, compensation keeps ICP nearly flat; only after reserve is used does pressure climb steeply.

test.q: On the ICP waveform, a P2 higher than P1 suggests:
test.explain: P2 (the tidal wave) reflects brain compliance; when it exceeds P1 the system is stiff and near decompensation.

test.q: Name the triad of hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing that is a late sign of raised ICP.
test.explain: Cushing's triad reflects brainstem compression and a desperate attempt to keep perfusing the brain.

test.q: Which type of brain edema responds best to corticosteroids?
test.explain: Vasogenic edema around tumors and abscesses comes from a leaky blood-brain barrier, which steroids help seal. Steroids do not help cytotoxic edema and are harmful in TBI.

test.q: Swelling of the optic discs from raised ICP is called ___.
test.explain: Raised pressure is transmitted along the optic nerve sheath, causing disc swelling seen on fundoscopy.

test.q: Why does a high blood CO2 level raise ICP?
choices: It constricts cerebral vessels and raises resistance
It dilates cerebral vessels and increases blood volume
It blocks CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations
It makes brain cells swell by drawing in sodium
test.explain: CO2 is a strong cerebral vasodilator; more blood in the head means higher pressure in a fixed box.

test.q: What is the term for the change in volume divided by the change in pressure?
test.explain: Compliance = dV/dP. Its inverse is elastance.

kidTest.q: The skull is like a:
kidTest.explain: The skull is hard and cannot get bigger in grown-ups.

kidTest.q: Which of these is NOT inside the skull?
kidTest.explain: Brain, blood and fluid are inside. Food goes to the stomach.

kidTest.q: If a bump of blood grows inside the skull, the pressure:
kidTest.explain: The box is full, so a growing bump makes pressure rise.

kidTest.q: At first, what moves out to make room?
kidTest.explain: Fluid and some blood can slip out first.

kidTest.q: Fill in: the skull is a hard ___ (a word for a container).
kidTest.explain: We compare the skull to a hard box.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors watch the pressure?
choices: It makes your hair grow faster
High pressure can squash the brain
It can change the color of your eyes
kidTest.explain: Too much pressure squeezes the brain and stops blood getting in.

advancedTest.q: A PRx (pressure reactivity index) that is persistently positive indicates:
advancedTest.explain: Positive correlation between MAP and ICP slow waves means vessels passively follow pressure; this is linked to worse outcome.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a large right temporal contusion has an ICP of 18 mmHg but a newly dilated right pupil. Best interpretation?
choices: The pupil finding is likely an artifact of monitor insertion
An ICP below 20 mmHg means herniation is not occurring
Focal mass effect can cause uncal herniation despite modest global ICP
The dilated pupil reflects optic nerve injury from the contusion
advancedTest.explain: Temporal masses sit next to the uncus and brainstem; compartmental gradients mean herniation can occur before global ICP is very high.

advancedTest.q: Marmarou's pressure-volume index is defined as the volume needed to:
advancedTest.explain: PVI is the volume that raises ICP by a factor of ten, a measure of craniospinal compliance.

advancedTest.q: Name the condition of raised ICP without a mass, often with transverse sinus stenosis, where vision loss is the main danger.
advancedTest.explain: IIH threatens vision through chronic papilledema; venous outflow narrowing contributes in many patients.

lessons.title: Herniation Syndromes

levels.kid:
Inside your head, the brain is split into rooms by tough sheets of tissue, a bit like walls in a house. There are small doorways between the rooms.

If something swells or bleeds in one room, it pushes the brain. A piece of brain can get squeezed through a doorway into the next room. Doctors call this **herniation**.

This is very dangerous, because the squeezed brain can press on the part that controls breathing and waking up.

One clue doctors look for is the eye. If one black pupil suddenly becomes big and does not get smaller in light, the brain may be squeezing a nerve. That means doctors must act fast!
levels.hs:
The inside of the skull is divided by stiff folds of dura:
- the **falx cerebri** runs between the two cerebral hemispheres
- the **tentorium cerebelli** is a tent separating the cerebrum (above) from the cerebellum and brainstem (below)

The **foramen magnum** at the skull base is where the brainstem becomes the spinal cord.

When a mass raises pressure in one compartment, brain tissue is pushed into another. This is **herniation**, a life-threatening emergency. Main types:
- **Subfalcine**: the cingulate gyrus slides under the falx. It can pinch the anterior cerebral artery, causing leg weakness.
- **Uncal**: the uncus of the temporal lobe slides over the tentorium edge and squeezes the **third cranial nerve** and midbrain. Classic signs: a **dilated, unreactive pupil on the same side**, drowsiness, and **weakness on the opposite side** of the body.
- **Central**: the whole upper brainstem is pushed straight down. Consciousness fades, breathing becomes abnormal and posturing appears.
- **Tonsillar**: the cerebellar tonsils are forced through the foramen magnum, crushing the medulla, which controls breathing and heart rate. This can cause sudden death.

Doctors treat herniation as a 'code' for the brain: raise the head, give a drug that pulls water out of the brain, get a CT and call neurosurgery.
levels.college:
**Subfalcine (cingulate) herniation** is the most common type and usually seen first on CT as midline shift. Compression of the **pericallosal branches of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA)** can cause infarction and contralateral leg weakness. It can also obstruct the foramen of Monro, trapping the opposite lateral ventricle.

**Uncal (lateral transtentorial) herniation:**
- Ipsilateral **CN III palsy**: the pupil dilates first because the parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor fibers run on the outer surface of the nerve; ptosis and a 'down and out' eye follow.
- **Contralateral hemiparesis** from compression of the ipsilateral cerebral peduncle.
- **Kernohan notch phenomenon**: the opposite peduncle is pushed against the tentorial edge, giving **ipsilateral** hemiparesis, a false localizing sign.
- **Posterior cerebral artery** compression can cause occipital infarction.
- Decreasing consciousness from midbrain reticular formation compression.

**Central (downward transtentorial) herniation** follows a rostral-caudal sequence: small reactive pupils and Cheyne-Stokes breathing (diencephalic stage), then mid-position fixed pupils and decorticate then decerebrate posturing (midbrain/pons), then ataxic breathing and flaccidity (medulla). Stretching of basilar perforators produces **Duret hemorrhages** in the midline pons and midbrain, usually fatal. Stretching of CN VI can cause a false localizing abducens palsy.

**Tonsillar herniation** compresses the medulla: neck stiffness, head tilt, bradycardia, hypertension and respiratory arrest.

**Upward transtentorial herniation** occurs with posterior fossa masses, particularly if supratentorial CSF is drained too fast by a ventricular drain.

**External (transcalvarial) herniation** is brain bulging through a skull defect such as a craniectomy.
levels.phd:
Herniation syndromes are a clinicopathological framework built largely from early twentieth century autopsy work and the bedside synthesis of Plum and Posner. Modern imaging has complicated the classic story in useful ways.

**Horizontal versus vertical displacement.** Ropper showed that the level of consciousness in acute hemispheric masses correlates better with **horizontal displacement** of the pineal gland and diencephalon than with downward displacement through the tentorial notch. Patients can be drowsy before the uncus is visibly herniated, and some patients with obvious uncal herniation on MRI remain alert. The tentorium is a two-dimensional idea; real brain moves in three dimensions.

**Why the pupil first?** The pupilloconstrictor fibers lie dorsomedially and superficially in the oculomotor nerve, close to its epineurium, and are vulnerable to compression by the uncus or a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Microvascular (for example diabetic) third nerve palsies characteristically spare the pupil because ischemia affects the core of the nerve.

**Tentorial anatomy varies.** The size of the tentorial incisura and the position of the brainstem within it differ between individuals, which partly explains why the same mass produces herniation at different volumes.

**Duret hemorrhages** are thought to arise from caudal brainstem displacement tearing or stretching paramedian perforators of the tethered basilar artery, though venous mechanisms have also been proposed.

**Paradoxical herniation** after decompressive craniectomy illustrates the role of atmospheric pressure: once the skull is open, atmospheric pressure acting on the scalp flap, combined with CSF loss (lumbar puncture or drainage), can push the brain downward despite low ICP, the so-called 'syndrome of the trephined' at its extreme.

**Imaging metrics** such as midline shift, basal cistern effacement and the relationship between shift and lesion thickness carry prognostic information and help gauge whether swelling is out of proportion to the visible mass.
levels.expert:
Herniation is a bedside diagnosis that must be acted on before the scan is back. A neurosurgical resident called to a newly blown pupil thinks in three tracks at once: temporizing measures, imaging, and the theatre.

**Immediate temporizing ('brain code'):**
- head up about 30 degrees, airway secured if consciousness is falling
- a hyperosmolar agent: mannitol or hypertonic saline
- brief hyperventilation as a bridge only, because prolonged hypocapnia causes cerebral ischemia
- correct coagulopathy if there is a bleed
- urgent non-contrast CT, then theatre or an external ventricular drain if indicated

**Exam pearls:**
- Confirm the pupil is real: a prosthetic eye, direct orbital trauma, previous eye surgery or nebulized drugs can mimic a blown pupil.
- A dilated pupil with ptosis in an alert patient with headache suggests a **posterior communicating artery aneurysm**, not herniation: that patient needs vascular imaging.
- Hemiparesis on the 'wrong' side may be Kernohan notch phenomenon; the pupil is the more reliable localizer for side of the lesion.
- Bilateral fixed pupils after herniation are an ominous but not always irreversible sign if treated within minutes, particularly in epidural hematoma.

**Posterior fossa is different.** Cerebellar hemorrhage or infarct can compress the brainstem and fourth ventricle with little warning. Small space, little reserve: these patients may go from talking to apneic quickly, so suboccipital decompression is often done early. Draining CSF from above in this situation must be cautious to avoid upward herniation.

**After craniectomy**, a sunken flap with worsening exam, especially after lumbar puncture or drainage, suggests paradoxical herniation: lay the patient flat or slightly head-down, stop drainage, give fluids and plan cranioplasty. Here, the usual reflex of giving an osmotic drug is the wrong move.

keyPoints: Dural folds (falx, tentorium) and the foramen magnum define herniation routes.
Uncal herniation: ipsilateral blown pupil (CN III) and contralateral hemiparesis.
Kernohan notch gives ipsilateral hemiparesis, a false localizing sign.
Central herniation progresses rostral to caudal; Duret hemorrhages are a late, usually fatal, sign.
Tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla and can cause sudden respiratory arrest.
Paradoxical herniation after craniectomy is treated by lying flat and stopping CSF drainage.

test.q: Which dural fold separates the cerebrum from the cerebellum?
test.explain: The tentorium cerebelli is a tent between the occipital lobes above and cerebellum below.

test.q: Classic uncal herniation causes:
choices: Contralateral dilated pupil and ipsilateral hemiparesis
Ipsilateral dilated pupil and contralateral hemiparesis
test.explain: The uncus compresses the same-side CN III and the same-side cerebral peduncle, which controls the opposite body.

test.q: In subfalcine herniation, the ___ gyrus slides under the falx.
test.explain: The cingulate gyrus herniates under the falx cerebri; this is seen as midline shift on CT.

test.q: Compression of which artery in subfalcine herniation can cause contralateral leg weakness?
test.explain: The ACA supplies the medial frontal lobe including the leg area of the motor cortex.

test.q: Why does the pupil dilate early in third nerve compression?
choices: The parasympathetic fibers lie on the outer surface of the nerve
The parasympathetic fibers lie in the deep core of the nerve
The sympathetic fibers in the nerve are cut by the compression
The optic nerve is compressed alongside it, causing an RAPD
test.explain: Superficial pupilloconstrictor fibers are the first to suffer from external compression.

test.q: Name the false localizing sign where hemiparesis appears on the same side as the mass.
test.explain: The opposite peduncle is pushed against the tentorium, causing weakness on the same side as the lesion.

test.q: Tonsillar herniation is especially dangerous because it compresses the:
test.explain: The medulla contains respiratory and cardiovascular centers; compression can cause apnea and death.

test.q: Name the midline brainstem bleeds caused by downward displacement in central herniation.
test.explain: Duret hemorrhages result from stretching of basilar perforators and are usually fatal.

test.q: Upward transtentorial herniation is a risk when:
choices: CSF is drained too quickly above a large posterior fossa mass
A patient sits up after a lumbar puncture with no mass
test.explain: Lowering supratentorial pressure fast lets a posterior fossa mass push brain upward through the tentorial notch.

test.q: Brain bulging out through a craniectomy defect is called external or trans___ herniation.
test.explain: Transcalvarial herniation describes brain pushing through a skull defect.

test.q: In central herniation, the earliest stage (diencephalic) typically shows:
choices: Small reactive pupils and Cheyne-Stokes breathing
Fixed dilated pupils with apnea and no reflexes
Normal consciousness with intact pupil reflexes
test.explain: The rostral-caudal sequence begins with small reactive pupils and periodic breathing before midbrain signs appear.

kidTest.q: Herniation means:
choices: Brain grows a brand new part inside
Brain gets squeezed into another space
Brain gets very happy and smiles
kidTest.explain: Part of the brain is pushed through a doorway into another room.

kidTest.q: What divides the inside of the head into rooms?
kidTest.explain: Tough sheets called dura split the space into rooms.

kidTest.q: Which eye clue worries doctors?
choices: Brown eyes that look nice and dark
Blinking a lot when you feel sleepy
One pupil gets big and won't shrink in light
kidTest.explain: A big pupil that ignores light can mean a nerve is squeezed.

kidTest.q: Why is herniation so dangerous?
choices: It tickles the brain and makes you giggle
It can press on the part that controls breathing
It makes you sneeze a lot during the day
kidTest.explain: The brainstem controls breathing and waking up.

kidTest.q: Fill in: when the brain is squeezed into another room, doctors call it ___.
kidTest.explain: Herniation means a part is pushed where it doesn't belong.

kidTest.q: When herniation happens, doctors should:
kidTest.explain: It is an emergency, so doctors move quickly.

advancedTest.q: A drowsy patient after craniectomy has a sunken skin flap and got worse after a lumbar puncture. Best first step?
choices: Give an osmotic drug and raise the head higher
Lay the patient flat, stop CSF drainage, give fluids
advancedTest.explain: This is paradoxical herniation driven by atmospheric pressure and CSF loss; osmotic therapy and head elevation worsen it.

advancedTest.q: An alert patient with sudden severe headache, ptosis and a dilated pupil most likely has:
choices: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing CN III
Diabetic microvascular third nerve palsy sparing the pupil
Uncal herniation from an expanding temporal hematoma
Horner syndrome from an internal carotid dissection
advancedTest.explain: Alert patients do not have herniation severe enough to blow a pupil; a painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy needs urgent vascular imaging.

advancedTest.q: Ropper's observations suggested that early decreased consciousness with a hemispheric mass correlates best with:
advancedTest.explain: Horizontal shift of the pineal and diencephalon correlated more closely with consciousness than uncal descent.

advancedTest.q: Why does a diabetic microvascular third nerve palsy usually spare the pupil? Ischemia mainly affects the nerve's ___.
advancedTest.explain: Superficial pupillary fibers are supplied by pial vessels and spared when ischemia hits the nerve's core.

lessons.title: ICP Monitoring & Management

levels.kid:
When a brain is badly hurt, doctors want to know the pressure inside the head all the time. So a surgeon puts a tiny sensor through a little hole in the skull. It works like a tire gauge that checks the air in a bike tire.

If the pressure gets too high, doctors use steps, starting with easy ones:
- lift the head of the bed
- keep the person calm, comfy and not too hot
- drain a little of the brain's watery fluid through a thin tube
- give medicine that pulls extra water out of the brain

If nothing works, surgeons can take off a piece of skull so the swollen brain has more room.
levels.hs:
In severe brain injury, doctors often monitor **intracranial pressure (ICP)** directly, because the patient is usually sedated and can't be examined well.

**Two main monitors:**
- **External ventricular drain (EVD)**: a thin tube passed through a small burr hole into a lateral ventricle. It measures pressure and can **drain CSF** to lower it. Main risks: infection and bleeding.
- **Intraparenchymal probe**: a fine wire with a sensor at its tip placed in the brain tissue. Easier to insert, but it can't drain fluid.

**Targets** in severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) guidelines:
- ICP below about **22 mmHg**
- cerebral perfusion pressure (**CPP = MAP - ICP**) of about **60-70 mmHg**

**Tiered treatment** (start simple, escalate if needed):
- **Basics**: head up about 30 degrees, head straight, sedation and pain control, normal oxygen and CO2, prevent fever, treat seizures.
- **Tier 1**: drain CSF through the EVD; give **hyperosmolar therapy** (mannitol or hypertonic saline), which draws water out of brain tissue into the blood.
- **Tier 2**: deeper sedation, muscle paralysis, mild hyperventilation for a short time.
- **Tier 3**: a medically induced coma with barbiturates, or **decompressive craniectomy** (removing a large piece of skull and opening the dura so the brain can swell outward).

Steroids are **not** used for swelling after head injury: a large trial showed they increased deaths.
levels.college:
**Indications.** Brain Trauma Foundation guidance supports ICP monitoring in salvageable severe TBI (GCS 3-8 after resuscitation) with an abnormal CT, and in some patients with a normal CT who have risk factors such as older age, motor posturing or hypotension.

**Devices compared:**
- **EVD**: the reference standard. It can be re-zeroed (transducer levelled at the tragus, approximating the foramen of Monro), drains CSF and allows CSF sampling. Risks include tract hemorrhage, malposition, occlusion and ventriculitis. Pressure is read with the drain clamped.
- **Parenchymal fiberoptic or strain-gauge probes**: lower infection and hemorrhage risk, accurate early, but zeroed only once before insertion, so they drift over days, and they cannot drain.
- Non-invasive estimates (optic nerve sheath diameter on ultrasound, transcranial Doppler pulsatility, pupillometry) help screening but do not replace invasive monitoring.

**Hyperosmolar therapy:**
- **Mannitol** creates an osmotic gradient and also improves blood rheology; it causes osmotic diuresis, so hypovolemia and kidney injury must be avoided. Serum osmolality and the osmolar gap are tracked.
- **Hypertonic saline** raises serum sodium (tracked in mmol/L) and supports blood pressure; risks include hypernatremia, hyperchloremic acidosis and, if sodium rises fast in chronic hyponatremia, osmotic demyelination.

**Hyperventilation** lowers ICP by vasoconstriction but reduces cerebral blood flow; prolonged or deep hypocapnia is avoided, especially in the first day when flow is already low.

**Refractory ICP:** barbiturates reduce metabolic demand and blood volume but cause hypotension, so vasopressors are often needed. **Decompressive craniectomy** (large frontotemporoparietal flap, at least about 12 by 15 cm, with duraplasty) relieves pressure. Prophylactic hypothermia has not improved outcomes in trials and is not routine.
levels.phd:
ICP-directed therapy rests on biologically plausible thresholds and observational association, but the trial evidence is more nuanced than textbooks once implied.

**BEST-TRIP (2012)** randomized patients in Bolivia and Ecuador to management guided by an ICP monitor or by serial imaging and clinical examination. Outcomes were similar. The trial did not show monitoring is useless; it showed that a protocol based on intensive clinical and imaging surveillance can perform similarly, and it fueled a consensus approach rather than a single number.

**Decompressive craniectomy:**
- **DECRA** tested early bifrontal craniectomy for moderate, diffuse ICP elevation. ICP fell and ICU days shortened, but functional outcome at six months was worse.
- **RESCUEicp** tested craniectomy as a last tier for refractory ICP. Mortality fell substantially, but more survivors lived with severe disability or a vegetative state. At twelve months more patients reached at least upper severe disability (independent at home). The ethical question, survival with what quality, is not answered by statistics alone and requires dialogue with families about values.

**Hypothermia:** Eurotherm3235 (therapeutic hypothermia as an early ICP step) showed worse outcomes; POLAR (prophylactic early cooling) showed no benefit.

**Consensus algorithms.** The **SIBICC** consensus (2019) codified tiers and introduced the **MAP challenge**: briefly raising MAP with a vasopressor and watching ICP. If ICP falls, autoregulation is likely intact and a higher CPP may help; if ICP rises, pressure-passive vessels suggest a lower CPP target. Later SIBICC work integrated brain tissue oxygen.

**Multimodality monitoring.** Brain tissue oxygen (PbtO2) probes, cerebral microdialysis (lactate/pyruvate ratio), PRx-derived optimal CPP and continuous EEG aim to individualize therapy. BOOST-II showed PbtO2-guided care was safe and reduced hypoxic burden; phase III trials (BOOST-3, BONANZA) are testing whether this improves outcomes.
levels.expert:
**Practical setup.** For an EVD, the transducer is levelled at the external auditory meatus (tragus) every time the patient is moved, because a few centimetres of height error changes the reading. Drains are clamped for accurate readings, and the drain height is set against the same reference to control how much CSF leaves. A dampened waveform means occlusion, air in the line or malposition until proved otherwise. Ventriculitis is suspected with fever, rising CSF white cells and falling CSF glucose relative to blood glucose (both measured in mmol/L).

**How an attending runs an ICP crisis:**
- First, check the reading is real: zero the system, look at the waveform, examine the patient.
- Second, look for a correctable cause: new or expanding hematoma, hydrocephalus, seizure, fever, hyponatremia, a kinked jugular, hypercapnia, agitation. A repeat CT is cheap compared with missing an evacuable clot.
- Third, escalate one tier at a time, giving each step time to work, and decide the ceiling of care early with the family.

**Pitfalls:**
- Pushing CPP very high with vasopressors and fluids can cause acute respiratory distress syndrome; CPP above about 70 mmHg is not routinely targeted.
- Mannitol in a hypovolemic trauma patient can drop blood pressure and CPP.
- Rapid sodium correction in a patient who was chronically hyponatremic risks osmotic demyelination.
- Barbiturate coma makes the neurological examination useless and complicates later brain death testing, because drug levels must fall first.
- After craniectomy, low ICP does not mean the brain is safe: watch for contralateral hematoma blooming once the tamponade is released, external herniation and subdural hygromas.

The best units treat the patient, not the monitor: numbers guide decisions, but trends, exam and imaging make them.

keyPoints: EVD is the reference standard: it measures and drains CSF but carries infection risk.
Parenchymal probes cannot drain or be re-zeroed after insertion and may drift.
Severe TBI targets: ICP below about 22 mmHg, CPP about 60-70 mmHg.
Tiered care: basics, CSF drainage and hyperosmolar therapy, then sedation/paralysis, then barbiturates or decompressive craniectomy.
Steroids increase mortality in TBI and are not used for ICP.
RESCUEicp: last-tier craniectomy lowered mortality but increased survival with severe disability.

test.q: Which ICP monitor can also drain CSF?
test.explain: An EVD sits in the ventricle, so it can measure pressure and remove CSF.

test.q: Where is an EVD transducer usually levelled (zeroed)?
choices: At the top of the head
At the tragus of the ear
test.explain: The tragus approximates the foramen of Monro, the reference point for intraventricular pressure.

test.q: The ICP treatment threshold in current severe TBI guidelines is about:
test.explain: Sustained ICP above about 22 mmHg is associated with worse outcome and is treated.

test.q: Mannitol and hypertonic saline are examples of hyper___ therapy.
test.explain: They raise blood osmolality, drawing water out of brain tissue.

test.q: Why are corticosteroids NOT used to lower ICP after traumatic brain injury?
choices: A large trial showed increased mortality
They raise arterial CO2 and dilate vessels
They are too costly for routine ICU use
They raise ICP by boosting cerebral flow
test.explain: The CRASH trial found more deaths with steroids in TBI.

test.q: Why is prolonged deep hyperventilation avoided?
choices: It causes vasodilation and raises ICP further
It raises metabolic rate and causes fever
It causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischemia
It overdrains the EVD and collapses ventricles
test.explain: Low CO2 constricts vessels; this lowers ICP but can starve brain tissue of blood.

test.q: Name the operation that removes a large piece of skull so the swollen brain can expand.
test.explain: A large bone flap is removed and the dura opened, giving the brain room to swell outward.

test.q: A main disadvantage of an intraparenchymal ICP probe is that it:
choices: Has a higher infection rate than an EVD
Cannot be re-zeroed after insertion and may drift
test.explain: Parenchymal probes are zeroed once before insertion and can drift over days.

test.q: CPP target in severe TBI is about 60 to ___ mmHg.
test.explain: Guidelines recommend CPP roughly 60-70 mmHg; higher targets increase lung complications.

test.q: Which class of drug is used to induce a coma for refractory ICP?
test.explain: Barbiturates lower brain metabolism and blood volume; hypotension is the main problem.

test.q: A main risk of mannitol is:
test.explain: Mannitol causes the kidneys to lose water; in trauma patients this can drop blood pressure.

kidTest.q: The pressure sensor in the head is like a:
kidTest.explain: It reads pressure like a gauge checks a bike tire.

kidTest.q: What is an easy first step to lower brain pressure?
choices: Lift the head of the bed
kidTest.explain: Raising the head helps blood drain out of the head.

kidTest.q: A thin tube can drain:
choices: Blood from the toes and feet
Some of the brain's watery fluid
Air from the lungs when you sneeze
kidTest.explain: A tube in the brain's fluid spaces can let a little fluid out.

kidTest.q: If nothing else works, surgeons can:
choices: Give the brain a big lollipop to lick
Take off a piece of skull to give room
Paint the skull a nice bright color
kidTest.explain: Removing a piece of skull lets the swollen brain bulge outward safely.

kidTest.q: Fill in: doctors put a tiny ___ in the head to read pressure.
kidTest.explain: A tiny sensor tells doctors the pressure all the time.

kidTest.q: Doctors use steps that start:
kidTest.explain: They start with simple steps and only escalate when needed.

advancedTest.q: During a SIBICC 'MAP challenge', raising MAP causes ICP to rise. This suggests:
choices: A blocked or drifting monitor; recalibrate before changing therapy
Obstructive hydrocephalus; place an external ventricular drain
Intact autoregulation; raise CPP further to shrink blood volume
Impaired, pressure-passive autoregulation; avoid pushing CPP high
advancedTest.explain: If ICP passively follows MAP, vessels are not reacting, so a lower CPP target is favored.

advancedTest.q: DECRA (early bifrontal craniectomy for diffuse injury) found:
choices: Lower ICP but worse 6-month functional outcome
Clear mortality benefit with better function
advancedTest.explain: ICP and ICU days fell, but functional outcome at six months was worse.

advancedTest.q: A patient's EVD waveform becomes flat and dampened. The FIRST thought should be:
choices: A truly normal ICP with stable compliance
Brain death with loss of arterial pulsatility
Occlusion, air or malposition of the system
Rising ICP needing barbiturate coma now
advancedTest.explain: A dampened trace is a technical problem until proven otherwise; check the system and patient before acting on the number.

advancedTest.q: Name the Bolivian/Ecuadorian trial comparing ICP-monitor-guided care with imaging and exam-guided care.
advancedTest.explain: BEST-TRIP found similar outcomes, showing protocol and context matter as much as the monitor.

lessons.title: Coma Examination

levels.kid:
When someone is in a **coma**, they look like they are asleep, but you can't wake them up, even by calling their name or gently pinching them.

Doctors are like detectives. They check:
- the eyes: do the pupils get smaller in a bright light?
- the eyes again: do they move when the head turns?
- blinking: does the eye blink if a soft cotton tip touches it?
- breathing: is it steady or strange?
- moving: does the person move an arm when pressed?

These clues tell doctors which part of the brain is in trouble. Sometimes a coma comes from a sugar or chemical problem in the blood, which doctors can fix quickly.
levels.hs:
**Consciousness** has two parts:
- **Arousal** (being awake), driven by the **reticular activating system** in the brainstem and its connections through the thalamus.
- **Awareness** (knowing yourself and your surroundings), which needs the cerebral cortex.

**Coma** is a state of unarousable unresponsiveness: eyes closed, no response to voice or pain beyond reflexes. It happens when the brainstem arousal system is damaged or when **both** hemispheres are affected. One small hemispheric lesion does not cause coma.

Causes fall into two groups:
- **Structural**: bleeds, strokes, tumors, trauma, herniation.
- **Toxic-metabolic**: low blood glucose, low or high sodium, liver or kidney failure, infection, drug toxicity, lack of oxygen.

**The coma exam:**
- **Glasgow Coma Scale** for eyes, words and movement.
- **Pupils**: size, equality and reaction to light.
- **Eye movements**: the doll's-eye test (oculocephalic reflex) or cold water in the ear (caloric test).
- **Corneal reflex**: blink when the cornea is touched.
- **Gag and cough** reflexes.
- **Breathing pattern**.
- **Motor response** to pressure: localizing, withdrawing, abnormal flexion or extension.

The first steps are always the same: protect the airway and breathing, check blood glucose right away, then get a CT scan of the head and blood tests.
levels.college:
**Localizing with brainstem signs:**
- **Pupils**: small and reactive (metabolic or diencephalic); pinpoint (pontine lesion, or opioid toxicity); mid-position and fixed (midbrain); unilateral dilated and fixed (CN III compression). Preserved pupillary reflexes in deep coma favor a metabolic cause.
- **Oculocephalic reflex (doll's eyes)**: turning the head makes intact eyes move the opposite way, staying fixed on a point. Never test until the cervical spine is cleared.
- **Oculovestibular (cold caloric) reflex**: with the head at 30 degrees and an intact tympanic membrane, ice water in one ear in a comatose patient with an intact brainstem causes **tonic deviation of both eyes toward the cold ear**. The fast corrective nystagmus is missing because it needs the cortex; its presence suggests the patient is not truly comatose.
- **Corneal reflex**: afferent CN V, efferent CN VII (pons).
- **Cough/gag**: CN IX and X (medulla).

**Respiratory patterns** (rostral to caudal): Cheyne-Stokes (bilateral hemispheric or diencephalic), central neurogenic hyperventilation (midbrain/upper pons, rare), apneustic breathing with inspiratory pauses (pons), cluster breathing, then ataxic breathing (medulla), which precedes apnea.

**Motor**: decorticate (flexion) posturing suggests lesions above the red nucleus; decerebrate (extension) suggests midbrain or pontine involvement.

**FOUR score**: eye, motor, brainstem reflexes and respiration, each 0-4. It works in intubated patients and can detect locked-in syndrome by asking for vertical eye movements and blinks.

**Mimics**: locked-in syndrome (ventral pontine infarct, awake but paralysed except vertical gaze and blinking), non-convulsive status epilepticus, akinetic mutism, catatonia and functional unresponsiveness.

Work-up: glucose, sodium, urea, liver tests, ammonia, blood gas (all in SI units such as mmol/L), toxicology, CT, EEG and lumbar puncture if infection is suspected and safe.
levels.phd:
Plum and Posner framed coma as a problem of anatomy: arousal depends on a distributed network from the upper pontine and midbrain tegmentum through thalamic intralaminar nuclei, hypothalamus and basal forebrain to the cortex. Lesion-network mapping studies have since localized coma-causing brainstem lesions to a small region of the upper pontine tegmentum near the parabrachial nucleus, functionally connected to the anterior insula and pregenual cingulate.

**Disorders of consciousness after coma:**
- **Unresponsive wakefulness syndrome** (formerly vegetative state): sleep-wake cycles and eye opening return, but there is no behavioral evidence of awareness.
- **Minimally conscious state (MCS)**: inconsistent but reproducible signs of awareness such as visual pursuit or command following. MCS minus and MCS plus are distinguished by language-related behaviors.
- **Emergence** from MCS is defined by functional communication or object use.

The **Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R)** is the reference standard; repeated assessments matter because single examinations misclassify a substantial fraction of patients.

**Covert consciousness.** In 2006 Owen and colleagues showed that a patient diagnosed as vegetative activated motor planning areas when asked to imagine playing tennis and spatial navigation areas when asked to imagine walking through her house, indistinguishable from healthy controls. This **cognitive motor dissociation** has since been detected with fMRI and EEG paradigms in a meaningful minority of behaviorally unresponsive patients, including in the acute ICU, and is associated with better long-term recovery.

**Mechanistic models** such as the mesocircuit hypothesis propose that loss of central thalamic drive to frontal cortex and striatum underlies impaired consciousness. This motivated thalamic deep brain stimulation trials and amantadine, which accelerated functional recovery in a randomized trial in traumatic disorders of consciousness.

**Prognosis after cardiac arrest** is now multimodal: no single test should drive withdrawal of care.
levels.expert:
**The first five minutes** of a comatose patient are about reversible causes:
- secure airway, breathing and circulation
- check capillary glucose immediately; hypoglycemia (for example below about 3 mmol/L) is corrected at once, with thiamine given in malnourished patients
- give naloxone if opioid toxicity is suspected (pinpoint pupils, slow breathing)
- look for signs of herniation and trauma, and protect the neck
- urgent non-contrast CT; add CT angiography if basilar occlusion is possible, because a basilar thrombosis is a treatable cause of sudden coma

**Exam habits of experienced neurologists:**
- Watch the patient before touching: spontaneous movements, myoclonus, eye position, breathing.
- Use central pain (supraorbital or trapezius pressure) to judge localization, and nail-bed pressure for limb responses; spinal reflexes can produce triple flexion that looks like withdrawal.
- Ask every 'comatose' patient to look up and blink twice. Missing locked-in syndrome is a devastating error.
- Subtle twitching of the face or eyes, or unexplained persistent coma, should trigger EEG for non-convulsive status epilepticus.
- Conjugate gaze deviation: away from the hemiparesis in a hemispheric lesion (eyes look toward the lesion), toward the hemiparesis in a pontine lesion, and away from an irritative seizure focus during a seizure.

**Prognostication after cardiac arrest** (European guidelines): wait at least 72 hours after return of circulation and normothermia, clear sedation, then combine predictors. Poor outcome is very likely when at least two of these are present: bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, bilaterally absent N20 waves on somatosensory evoked potentials, highly malignant EEG patterns, very high neuron-specific enolase, status myoclonus early, and diffuse anoxic injury on CT or MRI.

Beware the self-fulfilling prophecy: early withdrawal of care creates the poor outcomes that seem to prove the prediction.

keyPoints: Arousal needs the brainstem reticular activating system and thalamus; awareness needs the cortex.
Coma needs a brainstem arousal lesion or bilateral hemispheric dysfunction.
Preserved pupillary light reflexes in deep coma suggest a toxic-metabolic cause.
Cold calorics in coma with an intact brainstem: tonic deviation toward the cold ear, no nystagmus.
Always check glucose first and look for locked-in syndrome with vertical eye movements.
Cardiac arrest prognosis is multimodal and delayed at least 72 hours.

test.q: Arousal depends mainly on the:
choices: Corticospinal tracts in the spinal cord
Reticular activating system in the brainstem
Primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe
Dentate nucleus deep in the cerebellum
test.explain: The ascending reticular activating system and its thalamic relays keep the cortex awake.

test.q: Which lesion alone usually does NOT cause coma?
choices: A small lesion in one cerebral hemisphere
test.explain: Coma needs brainstem arousal damage or both hemispheres; one small hemispheric lesion is not enough.

test.q: Pinpoint pupils in a comatose patient suggest:
choices: A normal finding in light sedation
test.explain: Pontine lesions interrupt sympathetic pathways; opioids also cause miosis.

test.q: In a comatose patient with an intact brainstem, ice water in the right ear causes:
choices: Fast nystagmus to the left only
Tonic deviation of both eyes to the right
test.explain: The vestibulo-ocular reflex drives slow tonic deviation toward the cold ear; corrective nystagmus needs the cortex.

test.q: The corneal reflex uses cranial nerve V for sensation and cranial nerve ___ for the blink.
test.explain: Touching the cornea (CN V) triggers orbicularis oculi contraction (CN VII).

test.q: Name the condition where a patient is awake and aware but can only move the eyes vertically and blink.
test.explain: A ventral pontine lesion paralyses everything except vertical gaze and blinking, with preserved awareness.

test.q: Which test should NOT be done until the cervical spine is cleared?
choices: Corneal reflex with a cotton wisp
test.explain: Doll's eyes requires turning the head, which risks injuring an unstable spine.

test.q: Ataxic (irregular) breathing points to a lesion in the:
test.explain: Ataxic breathing reflects medullary respiratory center damage and often precedes apnea.

test.q: The ___ score rates eye response, motor response, brainstem reflexes and respiration and works in intubated patients.
test.explain: The FOUR score (Full Outline of UnResponsiveness) does not depend on speech.

test.q: Which bedside test should be done first in an unexplained coma?
test.explain: Hypoglycemia is quick to check and quick to fix, and it can mimic stroke or cause coma.

test.q: Which antidote reverses opioid toxicity?
test.explain: Naloxone is an opioid receptor antagonist used as an antidote.

kidTest.q: A person in a coma:
kidTest.explain: In a coma, calling or gentle pinching doesn't wake the person.

kidTest.q: Doctors shine a light in the eyes to see if the pupils:
kidTest.explain: Healthy pupils shrink in bright light.

kidTest.q: Doctors checking clues are a bit like:
kidTest.explain: They gather clues to find which part of the brain is in trouble.

kidTest.q: Some comas come from a problem with:
choices: The color of your hair and eyes
Sugar or chemicals in the blood
Shoelaces that are tied too tight
kidTest.explain: Low blood sugar can cause a coma and can be fixed quickly.

kidTest.q: Fill in: a deep sleep that you can't wake up from is called a ___.
kidTest.explain: That's a coma.

kidTest.q: A soft touch on the eye should make it:
kidTest.explain: The blink reflex protects the eye.

advancedTest.q: A 'comatose' patient after a basilar artery stroke opens the eyes and looks up when asked. The likely diagnosis is:
choices: Akinetic mutism from frontal lobe injury
advancedTest.explain: Ventral pontine infarction spares vertical gaze and awareness; always test vertical eye movements.

advancedTest.q: Owen's 2006 fMRI 'tennis imagery' study showed:
choices: Imagined tennis practice restores consciousness in most vegetative patients within weeks
Some behaviorally unresponsive patients can follow commands mentally (cognitive motor dissociation)
fMRI confirms brain death more reliably than clinical apnea and reflex testing
Most patients diagnosed as vegetative are fully aware but simply unable to move
advancedTest.explain: Brain activity on command revealed covert awareness in a patient behaviorally diagnosed as vegetative.

advancedTest.q: After cardiac arrest, when is neuroprognostication generally first appropriate?
choices: Within about 6 hours of return of circulation, before temperature management
At 24 hours after arrest, during cooling, with sedation still running
At least 72 hours after return of circulation and normothermia, sedation cleared
After a full year of observation, since earlier exams are uninterpretable
advancedTest.explain: Delaying and combining multiple predictors reduces false pessimism.

advancedTest.q: Name the drug shown in a randomized trial to speed functional recovery in traumatic disorders of consciousness.
advancedTest.explain: Amantadine accelerated recovery during treatment in patients with traumatic disorders of consciousness.

lessons.title: Brain Death

levels.kid:
Sometimes a brain is hurt so badly that it stops working completely and forever, even the deepest part that controls breathing. Doctors call this **brain death**. It is not the same as a coma, where the brain is still working a little and might get better.

To be sure, doctors do a very careful check:
- no response at all, even to strong pressure
- no eye reflexes or blinking
- no breathing on its own, even when the body needs air

A machine can still push air into the lungs, so the heart may keep beating for a while. But when the whole brain has died, the person has died. Doctors explain this very gently to the family.
levels.hs:
**Brain death**, also called **death by neurologic criteria**, means the **complete and irreversible loss of all brain function, including the brainstem**. In most countries it is legally the same as death, even though a ventilator can keep the heart beating and the body warm for a while.

It is very different from:
- **coma**, where the brainstem still works and recovery may be possible
- the **unresponsive wakefulness syndrome** (vegetative state), where the brainstem works, breathing is often spontaneous and the eyes open

**Before testing**, doctors must:
- know a catastrophic cause (for example massive bleeding, severe trauma or lack of oxygen)
- rule out things that can mimic it: low body temperature, very low blood pressure, sedating drugs, paralysing drugs and severe chemical imbalances

**The examination checks:**
- deep coma with no brain-driven response to pain
- pupils that do not react to light
- no corneal reflex, no cough or gag
- no eye movement with head turning or ice water in the ears
- **apnea test**: the ventilator is disconnected while oxygen is given, and doctors watch for breathing as CO2 rises. No breath means the breathing center is gone.

If the exam can't be finished, **ancillary tests** that show no blood flow to the brain can help.

Families need clear, honest words: the person has died. Organ donation, if appropriate, is discussed by a separate team.
levels.college:
**Prerequisites** (2023 US consensus guideline from neurology, pediatric, neurosurgical and critical care societies):
- an established, catastrophic, irreversible cause consistent with the findings
- core temperature at least 36 degrees Celsius
- adequate blood pressure (for adults, systolic at least about 100 mmHg or MAP at least about 60 mmHg)
- no confounding drug effect: sedatives cleared, neuromuscular blockade excluded with a train-of-four test
- no severe metabolic or endocrine disturbance that could explain the exam
- an observation period after the injury, longer after cardiac arrest (at least 24 hours after hypoxic-ischemic injury)

**Examination:**
- no response to central and peripheral noxious stimuli other than spinal reflexes
- pupils non-reactive (usually mid-position or dilated)
- absent corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular, cough and gag reflexes
- no facial movement to pain

**Apnea test:** preoxygenate, confirm normal starting CO2, disconnect from the ventilator while delivering oxygen, then check arterial blood gases. The test is positive (consistent with brain death) when there are no respiratory efforts and the **PaCO2 reaches at least 60 mmHg and at least 20 mmHg above baseline**, with acidemia. The test is stopped if blood pressure drops or oxygen falls dangerously.

**Ancillary tests** are used when the exam or apnea test cannot be completed safely (for example facial trauma, high cervical injury, severe lung disease). The 2023 guideline accepts tests of cerebral blood flow: four-vessel catheter angiography, radionuclide perfusion scintigraphy (the 'hollow skull' sign) and transcranial Doppler. They supplement but never replace the clinical exam.

**Spinal reflexes** can persist: triple flexion, the 'Lazarus sign' (arms lifting), toe flexion. They come from the spinal cord and do not exclude brain death.

Adults need one complete examination; infants and children require two exams separated by an observation interval.
levels.phd:
**History.** Mollaret and Goulon described 'coma dépassé' (a state beyond coma) in 1959, as mechanical ventilation allowed bodies to be sustained after the brain had failed. The 1968 Harvard ad hoc committee proposed criteria for 'irreversible coma' as a definition of death, and the US Uniform Determination of Death Act (1981) recognized death as either irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory function or irreversible cessation of all functions of the entire brain, including the brainstem.

**Whole-brain versus brainstem formulations.** The UK uses a **brainstem death** standard: irreversible loss of brainstem function, on the reasoning that the brainstem is necessary for consciousness and breathing. The US standard is whole-brain, yet in practice both rely on brainstem testing, since cortical function cannot be fully tested at the bedside.

**Conceptual debates:**
- Some brain-dead patients retain hypothalamic neurosecretion (for example no diabetes insipidus), which critics argue is a residual brain function. The 2023 guideline explicitly states that persistent neuroendocrine function does not preclude the determination.
- Prolonged somatic support for weeks or months in rare cases challenged the claim that brain death leads to rapid somatic disintegration; defenders shifted to a definition based on loss of the capacity for consciousness and breathing.
- Variability between hospitals in prerequisites, apnea thresholds and ancillary tests prompted the World Brain Death Project (2020) and the 2023 US revision to harmonize practice.

**Physiology after brainstem death.** Herniation provokes a catecholamine surge (hypertension, tachycardia, myocardial injury), followed by loss of sympathetic tone with vasodilatory shock, central diabetes insipidus, hypothermia, coagulopathy and inflammatory activation. Donor management (vasopressin, hormonal support, lung-protective ventilation) can improve the quantity and quality of organs transplanted.

**Ethics.** The 'dead donor rule' requires that donation does not cause death; separating the determination team from the transplant team protects trust.
levels.expert:
**How senior intensivists approach determination:**
- Treat it as a procedure with a checklist, not an impression. Most errors come from skipped prerequisites, not from the reflex exam.
- Be strict about confounders. Long-acting sedatives, barbiturate coma and therapeutic hypothermia after cardiac arrest prolong drug effect; wait, check drug levels when available or use an ancillary flow study. Severe hypernatremia (for example above about 160 mmol/L) or hypoglycemia must be corrected or explained.
- Distinguish spinal reflexes (stereotyped, triggered by stimulation of the limb or neck) from brain-mediated movements such as decerebrate posturing or eye opening, which exclude brain death.
- Watch for ventilator auto-triggering from cardiac oscillations or circuit leaks, which can mimic breathing; the apnea test settles it.

**Apnea test practice:** preoxygenate with high-flow oxygen, use continuous positive airway pressure or an oxygen catheter in the tube to prevent desaturation, draw blood gases every few minutes, and abort with an ancillary test plan if instability occurs. A high cervical cord injury makes the apnea test invalid.

**Communication.** Use the word 'died'. Phrases like 'brain dead but still alive on life support' confuse families and cause great distress. Explain that the ventilator moves air but the person cannot breathe or wake, invite family to be present for the examination when appropriate, and allow time. The time of death is the time the determination is completed.

**After determination:** if donation is planned, the organ procurement organization approaches the family; otherwise the ventilator is discontinued. Requests for continued support raise legal and ethical questions that vary by jurisdiction, so involve ethics and legal teams early and keep the conversation compassionate.

**Pediatrics:** neonates and children require age-adapted prerequisites and two examinations; the threshold for ancillary testing is lower in newborns.

keyPoints: Brain death is irreversible loss of all brain function including the brainstem, and is legal death in most countries.
Prerequisites: known catastrophic cause, temperature at least 36 degrees Celsius, adequate blood pressure, no drug, paralytic or metabolic confounders.
Exam: coma, absent brainstem reflexes and a positive apnea test (PaCO2 at least 60 mmHg and 20 above baseline, no breaths).
Ancillary tests of blood flow are used when the exam cannot be completed; they never replace it.
Spinal reflexes such as the Lazarus sign can persist after brain death.
Families should hear clearly that the person has died; donation is handled by a separate team.

test.q: Brain death means irreversible loss of function of:
choices: The cerebral cortex with the brainstem spared
One hemisphere plus the basal ganglia
The spinal cord below the foramen magnum
The entire brain including the brainstem
test.explain: Death by neurologic criteria requires loss of all brain function including the brainstem.

test.q: Which condition is NOT brain death?
choices: Absent brainstem reflexes and positive apnea test with prerequisites met
Unresponsive wakefulness syndrome with spontaneous breathing
Irreversible whole-brain loss confirmed by exam
test.explain: In the vegetative state (UWS) the brainstem works and breathing is often spontaneous.

test.q: Which must be excluded before testing?
choices: A known cause of the coma
A recent CT showing the injury
test.explain: Hypothermia, drugs, paralytics and metabolic disturbances can mimic absent brain function.

test.q: In the apnea test, PaCO2 should reach at least ___ mmHg with no breathing efforts.
test.explain: PaCO2 at least 60 mmHg and at least 20 mmHg above baseline is a strong stimulus to breathe.

test.q: A 'Lazarus sign' (arms lifting) after brain death is caused by:
test.explain: Spinal reflexes can persist and do not exclude brain death.

test.q: Name the test where the ventilator is disconnected to see if the patient breathes as CO2 rises.
test.explain: The apnea test checks the medullary respiratory center's response to high CO2.

test.q: Ancillary tests in brain death determination mainly show:
test.explain: Catheter angiography, radionuclide perfusion and transcranial Doppler show absent brain blood flow.

test.q: The core temperature should be at least ___ degrees Celsius before testing (2023 US guideline).
test.explain: Hypothermia depresses brainstem reflexes, so normothermia is a prerequisite.

test.q: Which phrase is best when talking to a family after brain death is confirmed?
choices: 'We are keeping him alive on life support.'
'He is brain dead but still alive.'
test.explain: Clear language avoids false hope and confusion; brain death is death.

test.q: Which country uses a 'brainstem death' standard rather than 'whole-brain' death?
test.explain: The UK defines death as irreversible loss of brainstem function.

test.q: A train-of-four test is used before brain death testing to exclude:
test.explain: Paralysing drugs abolish motor responses and must be excluded.

kidTest.q: Brain death means the brain:
choices: Is having a long and very funny dream
Is just tired and needs a good nap
Has stopped working completely and forever
kidTest.explain: All of the brain, even the breathing part, has stopped forever.

kidTest.q: Is brain death the same as a coma?
kidTest.explain: In a coma the brain still works a little and might get better.

kidTest.q: Which is part of the careful check?
choices: Asking the person a funny riddle
Looking for breathing on its own
kidTest.explain: Doctors check if the body tries to breathe without the machine.

kidTest.q: A machine can still push air into the lungs, so the heart may:
kidTest.explain: The machine keeps oxygen going, so the heart can beat for a while.

kidTest.q: Fill in: doctors explain this very ___ to the family.
kidTest.explain: Families are told with care and kindness.

kidTest.q: Doctors check the eyes for:
kidTest.explain: No eye reflexes is one sign of brain death.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a high cervical spinal cord injury and catastrophic brain injury needs brain death determination. Why is an ancillary test needed?
choices: The apnea test is invalid because the cord injury can stop breathing itself
Spinal reflexes in the limbs prove the brainstem is still functioning
Ancillary tests should replace the clinical exam in most trauma patients
Pupils are unreliable to examine after a high cervical spinal cord injury
advancedTest.explain: A high cord lesion interrupts the breathing pathway below the brainstem, so a failed breath does not prove medullary death.

advancedTest.q: Persistent hypothalamic function (no diabetes insipidus) in a patient otherwise meeting criteria:
choices: Does not preclude determination under the 2023 guideline
Excludes brain death under the 2023 guideline
Means the patient is in a coma
advancedTest.explain: The 2023 guideline states persistent neuroendocrine function does not prevent determination; critics see this as a conceptual tension.

advancedTest.q: After herniation, a typical physiologic sequence in a brain-dead donor is:
choices: Persistent fever and hypertension lasting until organ recovery
Immediate cardiac arrest, before blood pressure changes
Catecholamine surge, then vasodilatory shock and diabetes insipidus
Bradycardia and hypertension, then SIADH with fluid overload
advancedTest.explain: The sympathetic storm is followed by loss of tone, hypotension, DI, hypothermia and coagulopathy.

advancedTest.q: Who described 'coma dépassé' in 1959? Give either name.
advancedTest.explain: Mollaret and Goulon described this state beyond coma as ventilators spread.
